title: Income Statement & Comprehensive Income
description: Prepare and analyze income statement presentation, continuing operations and other comprehensive income.
html:
Purpose of the income statement

The income statement reports an entity's financial performance over a period of time.

At the CPA level, the important question is not simply whether an item increased or decreased equity.

You must determine whether the item belongs in net income, other comprehensive income, or directly within equity.

Revenues and Gains − Expenses and Losses = Net Income

CPA mindset

For every income-related item, ask:

  1. Is it recognized in the current period?
  2. Does it affect continuing operations?
  3. Is it part of discontinued operations?
  4. Does it belong in OCI instead of net income?
  5. Does it require separate presentation or disclosure?

Continuing operations

Most revenues, expenses, gains and losses recognized during normal business activity ultimately affect income from continuing operations.

Examples

  • Sales or service revenue
  • Cost of goods sold
  • Selling expenses
  • General and administrative expenses
  • Depreciation and amortization expense
  • Interest expense
  • Many gains and losses

Unusual or infrequent items

An unusual or infrequent event does not automatically get removed from continuing operations.

Material items may require separate presentation or disclosure so users can understand their nature, but unusual does not mean "outside net income."

CPA trap

Under U.S. GAAP, there is no separate extraordinary-items category.

Do not classify an unusual loss as an "extraordinary loss" simply because it rarely occurs.

Discontinued operations

Discontinued-operations reporting applies when the disposal or classification as held for sale of a component represents a strategic shift that has, or will have, a major effect on the entity's operations and financial results.

When the requirements are satisfied, discontinued operations are presented separately from continuing operations.

Income from Continuing Operations + Discontinued Operations, Net of Tax = Net Income

Important

Discontinued operations are generally presented net of applicable income tax effects.

Worked discontinued-operations example

Income from continuing operations before income tax: $500,000

Pretax loss from a qualifying discontinued operation: $100,000

Assume a 25% income tax rate for this simplified example.

Step 1 — Continuing operations

$500,000 × (1 − 25%) = $375,000

Step 2 — Discontinued operation

$100,000 × (1 − 25%) = $75,000 after-tax loss

Step 3 — Net income

$375,000 − $75,000 = $300,000

Comprehensive income

Net income does not capture every recognized change in equity arising from nonowner sources.

Comprehensive income includes both net income and other comprehensive income.

Comprehensive Income = Net Income + Other Comprehensive Income

Other comprehensive income

Certain items are recognized outside net income and instead enter other comprehensive income under the applicable accounting guidance.

OCI categories

  • Certain unrealized gains and losses on debt securities classified as available-for-sale
  • Certain foreign currency translation adjustments
  • Other items specifically required by U.S. GAAP to be reported in OCI rather than current-period net income

CPA trap

Not every unrealized gain or loss belongs in OCI.

Classification depends on the underlying accounting guidance for the specific item.

OCI versus AOCI

These terms are related but are not identical.

OCI

Other comprehensive income represents qualifying comprehensive-income items recognized during the current period.

AOCI

Accumulated other comprehensive income is the cumulative balance of OCI items reported within stockholders' equity.

Beginning AOCI + Current-Period OCI ± Applicable Reclassifications = Ending AOCI

Reclassification adjustments

Some amounts previously recognized in OCI may later be reclassified into net income when the applicable accounting requirements are satisfied.

A reclassification adjustment helps prevent the same economic effect from being counted twice in comprehensive income.

CPA mindset

When you see an OCI question, track both:

  • the current-period OCI effect, and
  • the cumulative AOCI balance in equity.

Presentation of comprehensive income

An entity may present comprehensive income in a single continuous statement or in two separate but consecutive statements, consistent with applicable presentation requirements.

Regardless of format, net income and the components of OCI must remain distinguishable.

Owner transactions are different

Comprehensive income concerns changes in equity arising from nonowner sources.

Contributions from owners and distributions to owners are therefore not components of comprehensive income.

Included in Comprehensive Income

Net income

Other comprehensive income

Not Comprehensive Income

Issuing common stock

Dividends to shareholders

Other owner contributions and distributions

Worked comprehensive-income example

Assume a company reports:

Net Income $240,000
Qualifying OCI Gain $30,000
Qualifying OCI Loss ($12,000)
Dividends Declared $20,000

Step 1 — Calculate OCI

$30,000 − $12,000 = $18,000 OCI

Step 2 — Calculate comprehensive income

$240,000 + $18,000 = $258,000

The $20,000 dividend is not subtracted when calculating comprehensive income because it is an owner distribution.

CPA trap

Dividends reduce retained earnings, but they do not reduce net income or comprehensive income.

Income statement relationships

  • Net income ultimately affects retained earnings.
  • OCI ultimately affects AOCI within equity.
  • Net income + OCI = comprehensive income.
  • Owner contributions and distributions are excluded from comprehensive income.

What you should know after this lesson

  • Understand the role of continuing operations.
  • Recognize that unusual items do not create an extraordinary-items category.
  • Understand the basic presentation of qualifying discontinued operations.
  • Distinguish net income from comprehensive income.
  • Distinguish OCI from AOCI.
  • Recognize major categories that can produce OCI.
  • Understand the purpose of reclassification adjustments.
  • Exclude owner transactions from comprehensive income.

quiz.prompt: A company reports net income of $310,000, an $18,000 qualifying gain in other comprehensive income, a $7,000 qualifying loss in other comprehensive income, and $25,000 of dividends declared. What is comprehensive income?
quiz.explanation: Net OCI is $18,000 − $7,000 = $11,000. Comprehensive income is $310,000 + $11,000 = $321,000. Dividends are owner distributions and are not components of comprehensive income.
